title: Πατρόκλου ἱκεσία
titleEn: Patroclus Begs for the Armour — Iliad 16.1–100
about: While the fighting goes on round the ship, Patroclus stands beside Achilles weeping like a spring. Achilles asks, in the likeness of a little girl pulling at her mother, why he cries, and whether it is news from home or pity for the Argives. Patroclus tells him that the best of the Achaeans, Diomedes, Odysseus, Agamemnon and Eurypylus, lie wounded among the ships, and calls him pitiless, born of the sea and the rocks. He begs to be sent out with the Myrmidons, in Achilles’ armour, so that the Trojans may take him for Achilles and give the tired Achaeans breathing-space; the poet remarks that he is begging for his own death. Achilles answers that he knows of no prophecy, and that his grief is the taking of his prize by Agamemnon. But he will not stay angry for ever, and he agrees: Patroclus is to put on the armour, lead the Myrmidons, drive the Trojans from the ships and then turn back, not going on to Troy lest Apollo or another god stop him. Achilles ends by wishing that no Trojan or Argive escape death but he and Patroclus alone take Troy.

sentences.t: ὣς οἳ μὲν περὶ νηὸς ἐϋσσέλμοιο μάχοντο·
sentences.l: So they, for their part, around the well-benched ship were fighting;
sentences.i: So they fought around the well-benched ship;
sentences.n: ὣς ‘so’ sums up the fighting of the last part, and οἳ μέν ‘they, for their part’ is answered by Πάτροκλος δέ at the start of the next line: the poet turns from the fighting to what is happening beside Achilles. The ship is not named; the last part ended with the fight at the ships, where Hector had laid hold of the stern of one. ἐϋσσέλμοιο ‘well-benched’ is the stock epithet of a ship, translated every time (σέλμα is a rowers’ bench). μάχοντο is the imperfect of μάχομαι without the augment.

sentences.t:
Πάτροκλος δ’ Ἀχιλῆϊ παρίστατο ποιμένι λαῶν
δάκρυα θερμὰ χέων ὥς τε κρήνη μελάνυδρος,
ἥ τε κατ’ αἰγίλιπος πέτρης δνοφερὸν χέει ὕδωρ.
sentences.l:
And Patroclus stood beside Achilles, shepherd of the people,
shedding hot tears, like a spring dark-watered,
which down from a sheer rock pours gloomy water.
sentences.i: But Patroclus stood by Achilles, shepherd of the people, shedding hot tears like a dark-watered spring that pours its gloomy water down a sheer rock.
sentences.n: Patroclus stands beside Achilles. παρίστατο is the imperfect middle of παρίστημι ‘stand beside’ and takes the dative Ἀχιλῆϊ. ποιμένι λαῶν ‘shepherd of the people’ is a stock phrase, translated every time. The last line of the simile stands word for word in Book 9 (9.15, iliad-052), where Agamemnon weeps; the line before it there reads δάκρυ χέων, without δάκρυα θερμά. μελάνυδρος ‘dark-watered’ is μέλας ‘dark’ plus ὕδωρ ‘water’. αἰγίλιπος is of unknown meaning (the old explanations are about goats); ‘sheer’ is the traditional guess, kept as in iliad-052. κατά with the genitive means ‘down from’. δνοφερόν ‘gloomy’ describes the water as dark and murky.

sentences.t:
τὸν δὲ ἰδὼν ᾤκτιρε ποδάρκης δῖος Ἀχιλλεύς,
καί μιν φωνήσας ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδα·
sentences.l:
And him, having seen, pitied swift-footed, heavenly Achilles,
and, lifting his voice, to him winged words he spoke:
sentences.i: When he saw him, swift-footed, heavenly Achilles pitied him, and lifting his voice he spoke winged words to him:
sentences.n: τὸν δέ ‘and him’ is Patroclus, the object of both ἰδών ‘having seen’ and ᾤκτιρε, the aorist of οἰκτίρω ‘pity’. ποδάρκης δῖος Ἀχιλλεύς is the stock name-and-epithet, translated every time (‘swift-footed’; the first part is πούς ‘foot’, the second probably ἀρκέω, not certain; δῖος ‘heavenly’). In the second line μιν is the pronoun ‘him’, here the masculine Patroclus. The line is the same as 1.201, where the same words are said to a goddess. The parts φωνήσας ‘lifting his voice’ and ἔπεα πτερόεντα ‘winged words’ are the stock phrases. The speech follows.

sentences.t:
τίπτε δεδάκρυσαι Πατρόκλεες, ἠΰτε κούρη
νηπίη, ἥ θ’ ἅμα μητρὶ θέουσ’ ἀνελέσθαι ἀνώγει
εἱανοῦ ἁπτομένη, καί τ’ ἐσσυμένην κατερύκει,
sentences.l:
“Why have you wept, Patroclus, like a girl,
a little child, who, running along with her mother, bids her pick her up,
taking hold of her gown, and holds her back as she hurries,
sentences.i: “Why are you in tears, Patroclus, like a little girl who runs along with her mother and bids her pick her up, taking hold of her gown, and holds her back as she hurries,
sentences.n: Achilles speaks. τίπτε is ‘why’ (τί ποτε), and δεδάκρυσαι is the perfect of δακρύω: the state of having wept, ‘you are in tears’. ἠΰτε ‘like’ begins the simile, which is the girl’s: ἥ is the girl, the subject of ἀνώγει ‘bids’, and ‘her’ in ‘bids her pick her up’ and in ‘holds her back’ is the mother, never named in the Greek. νηπίη, which elsewhere in our English is ‘foolish’, means here a small child, as the word literally says (‘not yet speaking’). θέουσ’ is θέουσα from θέω ‘run’. εἱανοῦ is a genitive because ἁπτομένη ‘taking hold of’ governs the genitive. ἐσσυμένην ‘hurrying’ is an accusative participle agreeing with the mother, the object of κατερύκει. The sentence goes on through the next two lines.

sentences.t: δακρυόεσσα δέ μιν ποτιδέρκεται, ὄφρ’ ἀνέληται·
sentences.l: and tearful she looks at her, until she takes her up;
sentences.i: and tearful she gazes at her until she takes her up;
sentences.n: This finishes the sentence about the girl: δακρυόεσσα ‘tearful’ is her; μιν is the mother. ποτιδέρκεται is πρός + δέρκομαι ‘look at’, and ποτι- is the epic form of προς-. ὄφρ’ ἀνέληται is ὄφρα with the aorist subjunctive of ἀναιρέομαι ‘take up’, the same verb as ἀνελέσθαι above; ὄφρα with this mood can mean ‘until’ or ‘so that’, and the English takes ‘until’.

sentences.t: τῇ ἴκελος Πάτροκλε τέρεν κατὰ δάκρυον εἴβεις.
sentences.l: To her like, Patroclus, a tender tear down you pour.
sentences.i: You are like her, Patroclus, shedding tender tears.
sentences.n: τῇ is the girl (the feminine dative ‘to her’), and ἴκελος ‘like’ takes the dative. The comparison is now stated outright. κατά belongs with the verb, a separated prefix (tmesis): κατὰ … εἴβεις is ‘you pour down’, from εἴβω. δάκρυον is singular, as often, meaning tears in general; τέρεν ‘tender’ agrees with δάκρυον.

sentences.t:
ἠέ τι Μυρμιδόνεσσι πιφαύσκεαι, ἢ ἐμοὶ αὐτῷ,
ἦέ τιν’ ἀγγελίην Φθίης ἐξέκλυες οἶος;
sentences.l:
Is it that something to the Myrmidons you are making known, or to me myself,
or some news from Phthia you heard, alone?
sentences.i: Is there something you are announcing to the Myrmidons, or to me myself, or have you alone heard some news from Phthia?
sentences.n: Achilles puts the possible causes of the tears as alternatives: ἠέ … ἢ … ‘is it that … or …’ (something announced to the Myrmidons, or to himself) and then ἦέ ‘or’ (news from Phthia). πιφαύσκεαι is the middle second person of πιφαύσκω ‘make known’, and the Myrmidons are Achilles’ own men. Φθίης is the genitive of Φθίη, the home of Achilles and Patroclus; the genitive can be ‘of’ or ‘from’ Phthia, and the English takes ‘from’. ἐξέκλυες is the aorist of κλύω ‘hear’ with the prefix ἐκ-, ‘hear out’, and οἶος ‘alone’ says that Patroclus alone has heard it.

sentences.t:
ζώειν μὰν ἔτι φασὶ Μενοίτιον Ἄκτορος υἱόν,
ζώει δ’ Αἰακίδης Πηλεὺς μετὰ Μυρμιδόνεσσι;
sentences.l:
Alive indeed they say still Menoetius, Actor’s son, is,
and alive is Aeacus’-son Peleus among the Myrmidons?
sentences.i: Menoetius, son of Actor, is still alive, they say, and Peleus, son of Aeacus, is alive among the Myrmidons?
sentences.n: Menoetius is the father of Patroclus, Peleus the father of Achilles. ζώειν is the uncontracted infinitive of ζώω (= ζῶ) ‘live’, after φασί ‘they say’; μάν is ‘indeed’. Αἰακίδης is the patronymic ‘son of Aeacus’. The edition prints a comma at the end of line 14 and the question mark only at the end of 15, so the two clauses are one sentence and one question; the English keeps them together and does not turn the first into a plain report. Line 16 states why these two lives matter.

sentences.t: τῶν κε μάλ’ ἀμφοτέρων ἀκαχοίμεθα τεθνηώτων.
sentences.l: Of these both, greatly we would be grieved, being dead.
sentences.i: We would be deeply grieved for the two of them, if they were dead.
sentences.n: τῶν … ἀμφοτέρων ‘these two’ are Menoetius and Peleus, and the genitive is the genitive of cause after ἀκαχοίμεθα ‘we would be grieved’ (aorist optative middle of ἀκαχίζω). κε with the optative makes it a possible case, ‘would’. τεθνηώτων is the perfect participle ‘dead’ (epic for τεθνεώτων) and carries the condition. ‘We’ is Achilles and Patroclus together.

sentences.t:
ἦε σύ γ’ Ἀργείων ὀλοφύρεαι, ὡς ὀλέκονται
νηυσὶν ἔπι γλαφυρῇσιν ὑπερβασίης ἕνεκα σφῆς;
sentences.l:
Or is it you who lament for the Argives, how they are perishing
at the hollow ships because of their own overstepping?
sentences.i: Or is it the Argives you are lamenting, how they are perishing at the hollow ships because of their own transgression?
sentences.n: The last of the alternatives: ἦε … ὀλοφύρεαι is the middle second person of ὀλοφύρομαι ‘lament’, here with the genitive ‘for the Argives’; σύ γε puts weight on ‘you’. Ἀργείων is one of the three names of the army, kept as the poet chose it. ὀλέκονται is ‘are being destroyed, perish’, and νηυσὶν ἔπι is ἐπὶ νηυσίν with the preposition set after its noun. ὑπερβασίης is ‘overstepping’, a going beyond the proper limit, and σφῆς ‘their own’ is the possessive of the third person plural: so the overstepping is the Argives’ own.

sentences.t: ἐξαύδα, μὴ κεῦθε νόῳ, ἵνα εἴδομεν ἄμφω.
sentences.l: Speak out, do not hide it in your mind, so that we may both know.”
sentences.i: Speak it out, do not keep it hidden in your mind, so that we may both know.”
sentences.n: The line is the same as 1.363, where Thetis says it to Achilles. ἐξαύδα is the imperative of ἐξαυδάω ‘speak out’; κεῦθε is the imperative of κεύθω ‘hide’, and νόῳ is the dative ‘in the mind’. ἵνα εἴδομεν is ἵνα with the subjunctive εἴδομεν (epic for εἰδῶμεν) of οἶδα ‘know’, and ἄμφω ‘both’ includes both speaker and Patroclus.

sentences.t: τὸν δὲ βαρὺ στενάχων προσέφης Πατρόκλεες ἱππεῦ·
sentences.l: Him, groaning heavily, you addressed, Patroclus the horseman:
sentences.i: Groaning heavily, you said to him, Patroclus the horseman:
sentences.n: The poet turns to Patroclus and speaks to him directly: προσέφης is the second person (‘you addressed’) where the usual line has προσέφη ‘he addressed’. The same line pattern appears at 1.364 with Achilles and Thetis. βαρὺ στενάχων ‘groaning heavily’ is a stock phrase. ἱππεῦ is the vocative of ἱππεύς ‘horseman’, a warrior who fights from a chariot, and is used here as a name-epithet of Patroclus. Patroclus’ answer follows.

sentences.t:
ὦ Ἀχιλεῦ Πηλῆος υἱὲ μέγα φέρτατ’ Ἀχαιῶν
μὴ νεμέσα· τοῖον γὰρ ἄχος βεβίηκεν Ἀχαιούς.
sentences.l:
“O Achilles, Peleus’ son, by far the best of the Achaeans,
do not feel resentment; for such grief has overpowered the Achaeans.
sentences.i: “Achilles, son of Peleus, by far the best of the Achaeans, do not feel resentment; for such grief has overpowered the Achaeans.
sentences.n: Patroclus speaks. The vocatives are ὦ Ἀχιλεῦ, Πηλῆος υἱέ ‘son of Peleus’ and μέγα φέρτατ’ Ἀχαιῶν ‘by far the best of the Achaeans’, with φέρτατος the superlative of φέρτερος ‘better’. μὴ νεμέσα is the second person imperative of νεμεσάω with μή ‘do not’: ‘do not take it ill, do not feel resentment’ at what he is about to say. βεβίηκεν is the perfect of βιάω ‘use force on, overpower’, with the Achaeans as object, and ἄχος is ‘grief’.

sentences.t:
οἳ μὲν γὰρ δὴ πάντες, ὅσοι πάρος ἦσαν ἄριστοι,
ἐν νηυσὶν κέαται βεβλημένοι οὐτάμενοί τε.
sentences.l:
For those indeed, all, who before were the best,
among the ships lie, struck and wounded.
sentences.i: For all those who were the best before now lie among the ships, struck and wounded.
sentences.n: Line 23 stands word for word at 11.825 (iliad-071), in the answer of the wounded Eurypylus to Patroclus, where the second line follows it too; that second line also stands in Nestor’s speech to Patroclus at 11.659 (iliad-070). οἳ μέν … πάντες is ‘those, all of them’, and ὅσοι πάρος ἦσαν ἄριστοι ‘who before were the best’. κέαται is the epic third plural of κεῖμαι ‘lie’. βεβλημένοι (‘struck’, by a missile) and οὐτάμενοι (‘wounded’, by a thrust) are perfect participles from different verbs.

sentences.t:
βέβληται μὲν ὃ Τυδεΐδης κρατερὸς Διομήδης,
οὔτασται δ’ Ὀδυσεὺς δουρικλυτὸς ἠδ’ Ἀγαμέμνων,
sentences.l:
Struck is he, the Tydeus’-son, strong Diomedes,
and wounded is Odysseus, famed-for-the-spear, and Agamemnon,
sentences.i: The son of Tydeus, strong Diomedes, has been struck, and Odysseus, famed for his spear, is wounded, and Agamemnon too,
sentences.n: The list of the wounded begins. βέβληται and οὔτασται are perfects, ‘has been struck’ (by a missile) and ‘is wounded’ (by a thrust). The article in ὃ Τυδεΐδης ‘he, the son of Tydeus’ goes with the patronymic; Τυδεΐδης is the son of Tydeus, here Diomedes. δουρικλυτός ‘famed for his spear’ is a stock epithet of several heroes, translated every time (it is δόρυ ‘spear’ plus κλυτός ‘famed’); the line is similar to one in Nestor’s speech (iliad-070), which reads δουρὶ κλυτός.

sentences.t: βέβληται δὲ καὶ Εὐρύπυλος κατὰ μηρὸν ὀϊστῷ.
sentences.l: and struck also is Eurypylus in the thigh by an arrow;
sentences.i: and Eurypylus too has been struck in the thigh by an arrow;
sentences.n: The same line as in Nestor’s speech in Book 11 (iliad-070),; the edition here prints a full stop. βέβληται is the perfect passive of βάλλω ‘strike’, κατὰ μηρόν is ‘in the thigh’, and ὀϊστῷ is the dative of the arrow, the instrument. Eurypylus is the fourth of the wounded leaders.

sentences.t:
τοὺς μέν τ’ ἰητροὶ πολυφάρμακοι ἀμφιπένονται
ἕλκε’ ἀκειόμενοι·
sentences.l:
These, for their part, the healers of many drugs are busied about,
healing their wounds;
sentences.i: The healers, skilled in many drugs, are busy about them, healing their wounds;
sentences.n: τούς ‘these’ are the wounded men just named, and the healers are the subject. πολυφάρμακοι ‘skilled in many drugs’ is φάρμακον ‘drug’ with πολύ- ‘many’. ἀμφιπένονται is ἀμφί ‘about’ + πένομαι ‘busy oneself’: ‘are busy about’ the men. ἕλκε’ is ἕλκεα ‘wounds’ with the last vowel dropped, and ἀκειόμενοι is the participle of ἀκέομαι ‘heal’. The line breaks at the raised stop; the rest of the line goes with the next unit.

sentences.t: σὺ δ’ ἀμήχανος ἔπλευ Ἀχιλλεῦ.
sentences.l: but you, Achilles, past all dealing with, have become.
sentences.i: but you, Achilles, have become impossible to deal with.
sentences.n: σὺ δέ ‘but you’ is set against the healers. ἀμήχανος is literally ‘without means’ and is said of a person who cannot be handled or got round; the English follows the way it is rendered of Nestor at 10.167, not the Odyssey’s ‘helpless’, which would say that Achilles lacks something, not that others lack a way to him. ἔπλευ is ἔπλεο, the second person of the aorist of πέλομαι, ‘you have turned out to be’.

sentences.t:
μὴ ἐμέ γ’ οὖν οὗτός γε λάβοι χόλος, ὃν σὺ φυλάσσεις
αἰναρέτη·
sentences.l:
May not me, then, this anger take, which you guard,
fearsome in your excellence;
sentences.i: May this anger that you cling to never take hold of me, you whose excellence is fearsome;
sentences.n: μὴ … λάβοι is the optative of wish ‘may it not take’, and οὗτος χόλος is ‘this anger’, which is Achilles’ anger, kept as χόλος ‘anger’ in the translation every time. ὃν σὺ φυλάσσεις ‘which you guard, hold on to’ turns the anger into something kept. αἰναρέτη is the vocative of αἰναρέτης, a compound of αἰνός ‘fearsome’ and ἀρετή ‘excellence’; the plain sense is ‘fearsome in your excellence’, and the tone is bitter, since the excellence is used only to hold a grudge.

sentences.t:
τί σευ ἄλλος ὀνήσεται ὀψίγονός περ
αἴ κε μὴ Ἀργείοισιν ἀεικέα λοιγὸν ἀμύνῃς;
sentences.l:
What will another be benefited by you, even one born late,
if you do not ward off unseemly ruin from the Argives?
sentences.i: What will anyone else gain from you, even someone born later, if you do not ward off unseemly ruin from the Argives?
sentences.n: τί σευ ὀνήσεται is literally ‘what will be benefited by you’, with σευ the genitive of σύ, and ἄλλος ‘another’. ὀψίγονος means ‘late-born’: someone of a later generation. αἴ κε μή is ‘if … not’, and ἀμύνῃς is the aorist subjunctive of ἀμύνω ‘ward off’, taking the harm (ἀεικέα λοιγόν, ‘unseemly ruin’) as object and the Argives in the dative, ‘from them’.

sentences.t:
νηλεές, οὐκ ἄρα σοί γε πατὴρ ἦν ἱππότα Πηλεύς,
οὐδὲ Θέτις μήτηρ·
sentences.l:
Pitiless one, not then to you at least was father the horseman Peleus,
nor Thetis mother;
sentences.i: Pitiless man, so Peleus the horseman was not your father after all, nor Thetis your mother;
sentences.n: νηλεές is ‘pitiless’. ἄρα with the imperfect ἦν marks a conclusion newly drawn: ‘so it turns out that he was not’. σοί is the dative of the person who has a father, and ἱππότα, the vocative-form nominative of ἱππότης, is ‘horseman’. Θέτις is Achilles’ mother, a sea goddess, which is what the next line plays on.

sentences.t:
γλαυκὴ δέ σε τίκτε θάλασσα
πέτραι τ’ ἠλίβατοι, ὅτι τοι νόος ἐστὶν ἀπηνής.
sentences.l:
but the gleaming sea bore you, and towering rocks,
since your mind is unkind.
sentences.i: the gleaming sea bore you, and towering rocks, since your mind is unkind.
sentences.n: The charge is that Achilles must have been born of sea and rock, since he is so hard. γλαυκή is the colour-and-shine word that also forms γλαυκῶπις (Athena’s ‘gleaming-eyed’), and is given the same ‘gleaming’; whether the sea is grey, blue-green or glittering is not fixed by the word. τίκτε is the unaugmented imperfect of τίκτω ‘bear’, ‘bore’. ἠλίβατοι ‘towering’ is a word of unknown meaning; ‘towering’ is the traditional guess, as in the Odyssey. ὅτι is ‘since’, and ἀπηνής is ‘unkind’, as always.

sentences.t:
εἰ δέ τινα φρεσὶ σῇσι θεοπροπίην ἀλεείνεις
καί τινά τοι πὰρ Ζηνὸς ἐπέφραδε πότνια μήτηρ,
sentences.l:
But if some prophecy in your own mind you are shunning,
and some one from Zeus your lady mother has pointed out to you,
sentences.i: But if you are shunning some prophecy in your own mind, and your lady mother has told you of one from Zeus,
sentences.n: These two lines are almost the lines of Nestor’s speech at 11.794–795 (iliad-070), with σῇσι ‘your own’ for ᾗσι, ἀλεείνεις ‘you are shunning’ for ἀλεείνει, and τοι ‘to you’ for οἱ. εἰ δέ … καί gives two conditions, both unanswered until the next line. ἀλεείνεις is ‘you are shunning, avoiding’. θεοπροπίη ‘prophecy’ is what a god has told in advance. ἐπέφραδε is the aorist of φράζω ‘point out’, and τινά ‘some one’ is a second prophecy, from Zeus, brought by Thetis. πότνια μήτηρ ‘lady mother’ is the stock phrase.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἐμέ περ πρόες ὦχ’, ἃμα δ’ ἄλλον λαὸν ὄπασσον
Μυρμιδόνων, ἤν πού τι φόως Δαναοῖσι γένωμαι.
sentences.l:
yet me at least send forth quickly, and along with me the rest of the people
of the Myrmidons grant, if somehow a light I may become to the Danaans.
sentences.i: then at least send me out quickly, and give me the rest of the Myrmidon troops to go with me, in the hope that I may somehow become a light to the Danaans.
sentences.n: This is the answer to the two conditions in 36–37: ἀλλά … περ ‘then at least’. πρόες is the aorist imperative of προΐημι ‘send forth’ and ὦχ’ is ὦκα ‘quickly’. ὄπασσον is the imperative of ὀπάζω ‘let follow, give as escort’, here with ἄλλον λαὸν Μυρμιδόνων ‘the rest of the Myrmidon people’; ‘to go with me’ is what ἅμα ‘along with’ says. ἤν πού τι is ‘if somehow, if perhaps’, and φόως ‘light’ stands for relief and safety. The text here prints ἃμα with a rough breathing, as the edition does.

sentences.t:
δὸς δέ μοι ὤμοιιν τὰ σὰ τεύχεα θωρηχθῆναι,
αἴ κ’ ἐμὲ σοὶ ἴσκοντες ἀπόσχωνται πολέμοιο
Τρῶες, ἀναπνεύσωσι δ’ Ἀρήϊοι υἷες Ἀχαιῶν
τειρόμενοι·
sentences.l:
And give me, on the two shoulders, your armour to arm myself in,
in case, taking me for you, they may hold off from the war,
the Trojans, and the warlike sons of the Achaeans may get breath again,
worn down;
sentences.i: And give me your armour to put on my shoulders and arm myself in, in case the Trojans, taking me for you, hold back from war and the warlike sons of the Achaeans, worn down, get their breath back;
sentences.n: This follows Nestor’s words at 11.798–800 (iliad-070), now in Patroclus’ own mouth: the first person for the second, though the request itself (δὸς δέ μοι … ‘give me …’) is worded differently there. δός is the aorist imperative ‘give’, and θωρηχθῆναι is the aorist passive infinitive of θωρήσσομαι ‘arm oneself’ (from θώραξ ‘breastplate’). ὤμοιιν is the dual dative ‘on the two shoulders’. αἴ κε is ‘in case, if perhaps’, with the two subjunctives ἀπόσχωνται (‘hold off, keep away from’, with the genitive πολέμοιο) and ἀναπνεύσωσι ‘get their breath back’. ἴσκοντες is ‘taking … for’ (a form of εἴσκω, ‘liken’). Ἀρήϊοι ‘warlike’ is ‘of Ares’, and τειρόμενοι ‘worn down’ is a passive participle of τείρω.

sentences.t: ὀλίγη δέ τ’ ἀνάπνευσις πολέμοιο.
sentences.l: and small is the breathing-space from war.
sentences.i: and the breathing-space from war is small.
sentences.n: The same line as in Nestor’s speech at 11.801 (iliad-070). ὀλίγη ‘small’ agrees with ἀνάπνευσις ‘breathing-space’, from ἀναπνέω ‘breathe again’. τε in δέ τ’ marks something that holds in general: a break from war is always short, which is why even a short one will serve.

sentences.t:
ῥεῖα δέ κ’ ἀκμῆτες κεκμηότας ἄνδρας ἀϋτῇ
ὤσαιμεν προτὶ ἄστυ νεῶν ἄπο καὶ κλισιάων.
sentences.l:
And easily we, fresh, men who are weary, with a battle-cry,
could push back to the town, away from the ships and the huts.”
sentences.i: And easily, being fresh, we could drive men who are tired out, with a battle-cry, back to the town, away from the ships and the huts.”
sentences.n: Almost the line of Nestor’s speech at 11.802 (iliad-070): there ὤσαισθε ‘you could push back’, here ὤσαιμεν ‘we could push back’, the aorist optative of ὠθέω, with κε giving ‘could’. ‘We’ are Patroclus and the Myrmidons. ἀκμῆτες ‘fresh, untired’ and κεκμηότας ‘tired out’ (perfect participle of κάμνω) are set against each other. ἀϋτῇ is the dative ‘with a battle-cry’, and κλισιάων is the epic genitive plural of κλισίη ‘hut’. The speech ends here.

sentences.t: ὣς φάτο λισσόμενος μέγα νήπιος·
sentences.l: So he spoke, begging, greatly foolish;
sentences.i: So he spoke, begging, and very foolish he was;
sentences.n: The narrator speaks. ὣς φάτο is ‘so he spoke’, the unaugmented imperfect of φημί. λισσόμενος is ‘begging’, the same verb as ‘begged’ in the previous part. μέγα νήπιος is an exclamation of the poet’s: νήπιος, literally ‘not speaking’, is the word for one who cannot see what is coming, and the next line says what it is. The text breaks at the raised stop.

sentences.t:
ἦ γὰρ ἔμελλεν
οἷ αὐτῷ θάνατόν τε κακὸν καὶ κῆρα λιτέσθαι.
sentences.l:
for truly he was going
for himself an evil death and death-fate to beg.
sentences.i: for in truth he was going to beg for an evil death and the spirit of death for himself.
sentences.n: ἦ γάρ is ‘for truly’. ἔμελλεν with the infinitive is ‘was going to’, with the sense of what was bound to come. λιτέσθαι is the aorist infinitive of λίσσομαι: ‘to beg for’, the object being θάνατον … κακόν ‘an evil death’ and κῆρα, the spirit that brings death, the death-fate, which is not the κῆρ ‘heart’ of another word. οἷ αὐτῷ is ‘for himself’, with οἷ the reflexive dative. The narrator tells us that Patroclus’ request will be his death.

sentences.t: τὸν δὲ μέγ’ ὀχθήσας προσέφη πόδας ὠκὺς Ἀχιλλεύς·
sentences.l: Him, greatly vexed, addressed swift-in-feet Achilles:
sentences.i: Greatly troubled, Achilles, swift of foot, said to him:
sentences.n: The whole-line speech introduction: τὸν δέ ‘him’ is Patroclus, the object of προσέφη ‘addressed’, and μέγα ‘greatly’ goes with ὀχθήσας, the aorist participle of ὀχθέω ‘be vexed, troubled’, a mood of annoyance and distress. πόδας ὠκὺς Ἀχιλλεύς ‘Achilles, swift of foot’ is the stock epithet, translated every time. Achilles’ answer follows.

sentences.t: ὤ μοι διογενὲς Πατρόκλεες οἷον ἔειπες·
sentences.l: “Oh me, Zeus-sprung Patroclus, what a thing you have said;
sentences.i: “Oh me, Zeus-born Patroclus, what a thing you have said;
sentences.n: Achilles speaks. ὤ μοι is an exclamation of distress, ‘oh me’. διογενές ‘Zeus-sprung’ is the epithet of heroes of high birth, translated every time; it does not say Patroclus is descended from Zeus. οἷον is the neuter accusative of οἷος and gives the exclamation ‘what a thing!’. ἔειπες is the aorist of εἶπον with the epic doubled vowel.

sentences.t:
οὔτε θεοπροπίης ἐμπάζομαι ἥν τινα οἶδα,
οὔτέ τί μοι πὰρ Ζηνὸς ἐπέφραδε πότνια μήτηρ·
sentences.l:
Neither of any prophecy do I take heed, any that I know,
nor has anything to me from Zeus pointed out my lady mother;
sentences.i: I take no heed of any prophecy that I know, and my lady mother has told me of nothing from Zeus;
sentences.n: Achilles answers the two conditions of lines 36–37 one by one. ἐμπάζομαι takes the genitive (‘take heed of’), and ἥν τινα οἶδα is a relative clause, with ἥν in the accusative as the object of οἶδα: ‘any that I know’. οὔτε … οὔτε ‘neither … nor’ links the two denials. The second is nearly the line of Patroclus’ speech (37) with the first person in place of the second: ἐπέφραδε ‘pointed out’ is the same verb.

sentences.t:
ἀλλὰ τόδ’ αἰνὸν ἄχος κραδίην καὶ θυμὸν ἱκάνει,
ὁππότε δὴ τὸν ὁμοῖον ἀνὴρ ἐθέλῃσιν ἀμέρσαι
καὶ γέρας ἂψ ἀφελέσθαι, ὅ τε κράτεϊ προβεβήκῃ·
sentences.i: But this fearsome grief comes upon my heart and spirit, whenever a man who is ahead in power wishes to rob his equal and take back his prize of honour;
sentences.n: The first line stands word for word in Book 8 (iliad-047), in Diomedes’ mouth. ἄχος ‘grief’ and αἰνόν ‘fearsome’ are translated as always. ὁππότε δή … ἐθέλῃσιν is the general ‘whenever’ with a subjunctive. τὸν ὁμοῖον ‘his equal’ is the object of ἀμέρσαι ‘rob’, and ἀφελέσθαι ‘take away’ with ἂψ ‘back’ has γέρας ‘prize of honour’ as its object. ὅ τε κράτεϊ προβεβήκῃ is ‘he who has gone ahead in power’ (the perfect subjunctive of προβαίνω): ὅ τε can be read as a relative (‘he who’) or as ‘because he’, and the English takes the relative.

sentences.t: αἰνὸν ἄχος τό μοί ἐστιν, ἐπεὶ πάθον ἄλγεα θυμῷ.
sentences.l: A fearsome grief it is to me, since I have suffered pains in my spirit.
sentences.i: That is a fearsome grief to me, for I have suffered pains in my spirit.
sentences.n: τό ‘that’ points back to what has just been said. μοί ἐστιν is ‘is to me’, and the grief belongs to the man who feels it. ἐπεί is ‘since’ and πάθον is the aorist of πάσχω ‘suffer’, here ‘I have suffered’. ἄλγεα ‘pains’ is the plural of ἄλγος, and θυμῷ the dative ‘in my spirit’.

sentences.t:
κούρην ἣν ἄρα μοι γέρας ἔξελον υἷες Ἀχαιῶν,
δουρὶ δ’ ἐμῷ κτεάτισσα πόλιν εὐτείχεα πέρσας,
τὴν ἂψ ἐκ χειρῶν ἕλετο κρείων Ἀγαμέμνων
Ἀτρεΐδης ὡς εἴ τιν’ ἀτίμητον μετανάστην.
sentences.l:
The girl whom as a prize to me the sons of the Achaeans picked out,
and with my own spear I won, having sacked a well-walled city,
her back from my hands took lord Agamemnon,
Atreus’-son, as if some unhonoured migrant.
sentences.i: The girl whom the sons of the Achaeans picked out as my prize of honour, and whom I won with my own spear when I sacked a well-walled city, her lord Agamemnon, son of Atreus, took back out of my hands, as though I were some unhonoured migrant.
sentences.n: The girl is Briseis, who is not named here. The sentence opens with her in the accusative and a relative (κούρην ἣν), which line 58, τὴν … ἕλετο ‘her he took’, picks up again; the English keeps the order. ἔξελον is the aorist of ἐξαιρέω ‘pick out, choose’, with γέρας ‘prize’ as the predicate. κτεάτισσα is ‘I acquired’, from κτεατίζω, and δουρὶ ἐμῷ is ‘with my spear’. κρείων Ἀγαμέμνων Ἀτρεΐδης ‘lord Agamemnon, son of Atreus’ is the stock name. The last line is the one in Book 9 (iliad-057), where Achilles says it too: ὡς εἴ τιν’ ἀτίμητον μετανάστην is ‘as if (I were) some unhonoured migrant’, a man with no rights in the place he has moved to.

sentences.t: ἀλλὰ τὰ μὲν προτετύχθαι ἐάσομεν·
sentences.l: But these things, for their part, to have been done before we shall let be;
sentences.i: But we shall let those things lie, as done and past;
sentences.n: ἀλλά turns from the grievance. προτετύχθαι is the perfect passive infinitive of προτεύχω, ‘to have been made, done beforehand’, so ‘what has been done’, and ἐάσομεν is ‘we shall let’ (ἐάω): the future tense carries a decision, not just a prediction. The ‘we’ is general (‘let us’). The line breaks at the raised stop.

sentences.t:
οὐδ’ ἄρα πως ἦν
ἀσπερχὲς κεχολῶσθαι ἐνὶ φρεσίν·
sentences.l:
and it was not, it seems, in any way possible
to be angry unceasingly in the heart;
sentences.i: and it was not, after all, possible to stay angry without pause in my heart;
sentences.n: οὐδ’ ἄρα πως ἦν is ‘and it was not, it turns out, in any way (possible)’, with ἦν ‘it was possible’ taking an infinitive. κεχολῶσθαι is the perfect middle infinitive of χολόομαι, ‘to be angered’, a state that has been entered and goes on. ἀσπερχές ‘unceasingly, without pause’ is an adverb. ἐνὶ φρεσίν is ‘in the heart, in the mind’.

sentences.t:
ἤτοι ἔφην γε
οὐ πρὶν μηνιθμὸν καταπαυσέμεν, ἀλλ’ ὁπότ’ ἂν δὴ
νῆας ἐμὰς ἀφίκηται ἀϋτή τε πτόλεμός τε.
sentences.l:
indeed I said, at least,
that not before would I stop my wrath, until, when
to my ships the battle-cry and war should come.
sentences.i: I did say, indeed, that I would not put an end to my wrath before the time when the battle-cry and the war should reach my own ships.
sentences.n: ἤτοι ἔφην γε is ‘indeed I said’. καταπαυσέμεν is the future infinitive of καταπαύω ‘stop’, in indirect speech after ἔφην, and οὐ πρὶν … ἀλλ’ ὁπότ’ ἂν is ‘not before … but when’. μηνιθμός is a noun for the state of being wrathful, related to μῆνις and μηνίω; the English gives ‘wrath’. ἀφίκηται is the aorist subjunctive of ἀφικνέομαι ‘reach’, in the singular with two subjects, ἀϋτή ‘battle-cry’ and πτόλεμος, the poet’s form of πόλεμος ‘war’. Achilles said as much to Ajax in Book 9 (9.650–653, iliad-057): he would not think of fighting until Hector reached the huts and ships of the Myrmidons.

sentences.t:
τύνη δ’ ὤμοιιν μὲν ἐμὰ κλυτὰ τεύχεα δῦθι,
ἄρχε δὲ Μυρμιδόνεσσι φιλοπτολέμοισι μάχεσθαι,
sentences.l:
But you, on your shoulders my famous armour put on,
and begin, for the war-loving Myrmidons, to fight,
sentences.i: But you, put my famous armour on your shoulders, and lead the war-loving Myrmidons into the fight,
sentences.n: τύνη is the emphatic ‘you’ (= σύ), and δῦθι is the aorist imperative of δύω ‘get into, put on’, with τεύχεα ‘armour’ and ὤμοιιν ‘on the two shoulders’ (a dual). μέν in ὤμοιιν μέν is answered by δέ in ἄρχε δέ ‘and begin, lead’. ἄρχε with the infinitive μάχεσθαι is ‘lead the fighting’, with Μυρμιδόνεσσι the men he leads; the dative is loosely used, and the English says ‘lead … into the fight’. φιλοπτολέμοισι is φίλος and πτόλεμος: ‘war-loving’, an epithet used of the Myrmidons here and of the Trojans below.

sentences.t:
εἰ δὴ κυάνεον Τρώων νέφος ἀμφιβέβηκε
νηυσὶν ἐπικρατέως, οἳ δὲ ῥηγμῖνι θαλάσσης
κεκλίαται, χώρης ὀλίγην ἔτι μοῖραν ἔχοντες
Ἀργεῖοι, Τρώων δὲ πόλις ἐπὶ πᾶσα βέβηκε
θάρσυνος·
sentences.l:
if indeed a dark cloud of Trojans has come around the ships
mightily, and those on the surf-line of the sea
are leaning, keeping a small portion still of land,
the Argives, and the whole city of the Trojans has come upon them
bold;
sentences.i: if indeed a dark cloud of Trojans has come around the ships mightily, and the Argives, who still hold only a small portion of ground, are leaning against the shore where the sea breaks, and the whole city of the Trojans has come upon them emboldened;
sentences.n: εἰ δή ‘if indeed’ states a fact as ground for what was asked: given that this is so. κυάνεον … νέφος Τρώων ‘a dark cloud of Trojans’ is a metaphor for the massed army, and ἀμφιβέβηκε is the perfect ‘has come around’. ἐπικρατέως is ‘mightily, with mastery’, from κράτος ‘power’. κεκλίαται is the perfect middle of κλίνω ‘lean’, in the third plural: the Argives are ‘leaning’ on the beach, the picture of men backed up against the sea; ‘leaning against’ in the English keeps the verb, and the Greek does not say that they are pressed or driven. ῥηγμῖνι θαλάσσης is the surf-line of the sea, the place where it breaks on the shore. χώρης ὀλίγην … μοῖραν is ‘a small portion of land’. ἐπὶ … βέβηκε is a separated prefix (tmesis), ‘has come upon’. θάρσυνος is a word formed on θάρσος ‘courage’; the English gives ‘emboldened’; the exact force of the word is not known beyond its form, and the reason (that Achilles stays out) comes from the next lines.

sentences.t:
οὐ γὰρ ἐμῆς κόρυθος λεύσσουσι μέτωπον
ἐγγύθι λαμπομένης·
sentences.l:
for they do not see the brow of my helmet
shining close by;
sentences.i: for they do not see the brow of my helmet shining close by;
sentences.n: οὐ γάρ explains why the Trojans are bold. λεύσσουσι is ‘they look at, see’, the object μέτωπον being the ‘front, brow’ of the helmet, and λαμπομένης ‘shining’ agrees with κόρυθος ‘helmet’. ἐγγύθι is ‘close by, near’. The picture is that the helmet is not before the Trojans’ eyes.

sentences.t:
τάχα κεν φεύγοντες ἐναύλους
πλήσειαν νεκύων, εἴ μοι κρείων Ἀγαμέμνων
ἤπια εἰδείη·
sentences.i: Fleeing, they would soon fill the stream-beds with corpses, if lord Agamemnon were kindly disposed to me;
sentences.n: τάχα κεν … πλήσειαν is ‘soon they would fill’, the optative with κεν, and νεκύων ‘with corpses’ is the genitive of what fills. ἐναύλους is a rare noun for water-courses; ‘stream-beds’ is the sense of its parts (ἐν and αὐλός ‘pipe’, a channel) and not certain. εἰ … εἰδείη is the optative of οἶδα, and ἤπια εἰδείη is the set phrase ‘to know kindly things’, to be kindly disposed, with μοι ‘to me’. κρείων Ἀγαμέμνων is ‘lord Agamemnon’. The line breaks at the raised stop.

sentences.t: νῦν δὲ στρατὸν ἀμφιμάχονται.
sentences.l: but now they fight around the army.
sentences.i: but as it is, they are fighting around the army.
sentences.n: νῦν δέ is ‘but as things are’, the contrast with the wish that has just been made (‘if Agamemnon were kind … but now’). ἀμφιμάχονται is ἀμφί ‘around’ + μάχομαι ‘fight’ with the accusative στρατόν ‘army’. The subject is the Trojans, and the army is the Achaean host.

sentences.t:
οὐ γὰρ Τυδεΐδεω Διομήδεος ἐν παλάμῃσι
μαίνεται ἐγχείη Δαναῶν ἀπὸ λοιγὸν ἀμῦναι·
sentences.l:
For not in the hands of Tydeus’-son Diomedes
rages the spear to ward ruin off from the Danaans;
sentences.i: For the spear does not rage in the hands of Diomedes, son of Tydeus, to ward ruin off from the Danaans;
sentences.n: Achilles lists those who cannot help. Τυδεΐδεω Διομήδεος is ‘Diomedes, Tydeus’ son’, with the epic genitive -εω, one syllable in the metre. ἐν παλάμῃσι is ‘in the hands’, the epic dative plural. μαίνεται is ‘rages’, of the spear as if alive. ἀμῦναι is the aorist infinitive of ἀμύνω ‘ward off’, giving the purpose, and Δαναῶν ἀπό is ἀπὸ Δαναῶν with the preposition after its noun. Δαναῶν is one of the three names of the army, as the poet chose it. λοιγόν is ‘ruin’.

sentences.t:
οὐδέ πω Ἀτρεΐδεω ὀπὸς ἔκλυον αὐδήσαντος
ἐχθρῆς ἐκ κεφαλῆς·
sentences.l:
nor yet have I heard the voice of Atreus’-son speaking
from his hateful head;
sentences.i: nor have I yet heard the voice of the son of Atreus speaking from his hateful head;
sentences.n: ὀπός here is the genitive of ὄψ ‘voice’, the thing heard (verbs of hearing take the genitive), not the plant-juice ὀπός; the ‘of Atreus’-son’ and ‘speaking’ (αὐδήσαντος, the aorist participle of αὐδάω ‘speak’) are in the genitive too. ἔκλυον is the aorist of κλύω ‘hear’, and οὐδέ πω is ‘nor yet’. ἐχθρῆς ἐκ κεφαλῆς is ‘from his hateful head’: the head stands for the man, and ἐχθρῆς is Achilles’ contempt for Agamemnon. The line breaks at the raised stop.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ Ἕκτορος ἀνδροφόνοιο
Τρωσὶ κελεύοντος περιάγνυται, οἳ δ’ ἀλαλητῷ
πᾶν πεδίον κατέχουσι μάχῃ νικῶντες Ἀχαιούς.
sentences.l:
but of man-slaying Hector,
urging on the Trojans, the voice breaks round, and they with an outcry
hold the whole plain, conquering the Achaeans in battle.
sentences.i: but it is the voice of man-slaying Hector, urging on the Trojans, that bursts all round, and they with an outcry hold the whole plain, overcoming the Achaeans in battle.
sentences.n: The missing subject of περιάγνυται is a nominative ‘voice’ (ὄψ), understood from the ὀπός of the line before, which stands in the genitive there: Agamemnon’s voice is not heard, Hector’s is. περιάγνυται is the middle of περιάγνυμι, περί ‘around’ + ἄγνυμι ‘break’; of a voice it means something like ‘breaks out all round’, and the exact sense is not known beyond the parts. ἀνδροφόνοιο ‘man-slaying’ is Hector’s stock epithet, translated every time. κελεύοντος ‘urging on’ takes the dative Τρωσί. οἳ δέ are the Trojans, ἀλαλητῷ ‘with an outcry’ is a dative of manner, and κατέχουσι is ‘hold, occupy’. νικῶντες Ἀχαιούς is ‘overcoming the Achaeans’, and μάχῃ is the dative ‘in battle’.

sentences.t:
ἀλλὰ καὶ ὧς Πάτροκλε νεῶν ἄπο λοιγὸν ἀμύνων
ἔμπεσ’ ἐπικρατέως, μὴ δὴ πυρὸς αἰθομένοιο
νῆας ἐνιπρήσωσι, φίλον δ’ ἀπὸ νόστον ἕλωνται.
sentences.l:
But even so, Patroclus, warding ruin from the ships,
fall on them mightily, lest with blazing fire
they burn the ships, and take away the dear homecoming.
sentences.i: But even so, Patroclus, fall on them mightily, warding ruin off from the ships, so that they do not burn the ships with blazing fire and take away our dear homecoming.
sentences.n: ἀλλὰ καὶ ὥς is ‘but even so, even as things are’. ἔμπεσ’ is the aorist imperative of ἐμπίπτω ‘fall on’, the object (‘them’, the Trojans) not stated. ἀμύνων is ‘warding off’ ruin (λοιγόν) from the ships (νεῶν ἄπο), as in the line above. μὴ δή … ἐνιπρήσωσι is a fear clause (‘lest they burn’, the aorist subjunctive of ἐμπίπρημι), with πυρὸς αἰθομένοιο ‘with blazing fire’ as a genitive of means. ἀπὸ … ἕλωνται is ἀφέλωνται separated (tmesis): ‘take away’ the νόστος ‘homecoming’. φίλον ‘dear’ can also mean ‘one’s own’; the ‘our’ in the English is the sense, since it is the Achaeans’ homecoming that is at stake.

sentences.t:
πείθεο δ’ ὥς τοι ἐγὼ μύθου τέλος ἐν φρεσὶ θείω,
ὡς ἄν μοι τιμὴν μεγάλην καὶ κῦδος ἄρηαι
πρὸς πάντων Δαναῶν, ἀτὰρ οἳ περικαλλέα κούρην
ἂψ ἀπονάσσωσιν, ποτὶ δ’ ἀγλαὰ δῶρα πόρωσιν.
sentences.l:
And obey, as I shall lay the end of the word in your mind,
so that for me great honour and glory you may win
from all the Danaans, and that they the very beautiful girl
back may send, and splendid gifts besides may give.
sentences.i: And obey me, as I set in your mind the purpose of my word, so that you may win me great honour and glory from all the Danaans, and they may send the very beautiful girl back and give splendid gifts besides.
sentences.n: πείθεο is the imperative of πείθομαι ‘obey’. ὥς … θείω is the aorist subjunctive of τίθημι: ‘as I shall put in your mind the end of the word’, that is, the purpose of what Achilles is saying; the instructions that follow spell it out. ὡς ἄν … ἄρηαι is the aorist subjunctive of ἄρνυμαι ‘win’, and μοι is ‘for me’. The second clause, ἀτὰρ οἳ … ἀπονάσσωσιν, has the Danaans as subject: ἀπονάσσω is a rare verb (‘cause to dwell away, send away’), so ‘send back’ with ἂψ ‘back’; ‘to me’ is understood. ἀγλαά is ‘splendid’, and ποτί, here an adverb ‘besides, in addition’, goes with πόρωσιν ‘give’. περικαλλέα ‘very beautiful’ is περί ‘exceedingly’ + κάλλος ‘beauty’.

sentences.t: ἐκ νηῶν ἐλάσας ἰέναι πάλιν·
sentences.l: Having driven them from the ships, come back again;
sentences.i: Once you have driven them from the ships, come back;
sentences.n: ἰέναι is an infinitive used as an imperative, ‘go, return’, and πάλιν is ‘back’. ἐλάσας is the aorist participle of ἐλαύνω ‘drive’, the object (the Trojans) not stated. The line breaks at the raised stop.

sentences.t:
εἰ δέ κεν αὖ τοι
δώῃ κῦδος ἀρέσθαι ἐρίγδουπος πόσις Ἥρης,
μὴ σύ γ’ ἄνευθεν ἐμεῖο λιλαίεσθαι πολεμίζειν
Τρωσὶ φιλοπτολέμοισιν·
sentences.l:
but if in turn to you the loud-crashing husband of Hera
grants to win glory,
do not you, at least, without me be eager to make war
on the war-loving Trojans;
sentences.i: but if the loud-crashing husband of Hera in turn grants you to win glory, do not be eager to make war on the war-loving Trojans without me;
sentences.n: εἰ δέ κεν αὖ is ‘but if in turn’, and δώῃ is the aorist subjunctive of δίδωμι, ‘should give’, with κῦδος ἀρέσθαι ‘to win glory’ (the aorist infinitive of ἄρνυμαι, the verb of ἄρηαι in the line above). ἐρίγδουπος πόσις Ἥρης ‘loud-crashing husband of Hera’ is Zeus, translated every time. μή with the infinitive λιλαίεσθαι ‘be eager’ is a prohibition. ἄνευθεν ἐμεῖο is ‘apart from me’, and Τρωσὶ φιλοπτολέμοισιν ‘the war-loving Trojans’ is a dative of the opponents, with the same compound as for the Myrmidons above.

sentences.t: ἀτιμότερον δέ με θήσεις·
sentences.l: and more dishonoured me you will make;
sentences.i: you will make me more dishonoured;
sentences.n: ἀτιμότερον is the comparative of ἄτιμος ‘dishonoured’, and θήσεις ‘you will make’ (a future of τίθημι) governs με and the adjective. The comparison is with his present dishonour.

sentences.t:
μὴ δ’ ἐπαγαλλόμενος πολέμῳ καὶ δηϊοτῆτι
Τρῶας ἐναιρόμενος προτὶ Ἴλιον ἡγεμονεύειν,
μή τις ἀπ’ Οὐλύμποιο θεῶν αἰειγενετάων
ἐμβήῃ·
sentences.l:
and not, exulting in war and fighting,
slaying Trojans, to lead on toward Ilium,
lest one from Olympus of the gods, the forever-born,
step in;
sentences.i: and do not, exulting in war and fighting, slaying Trojans, take the lead toward Ilium, lest one of the everlasting gods step in from Olympus;
sentences.n: μηδέ with the infinitive ἡγεμονεύειν ‘take the lead’ goes on the prohibition of line 89. ἐπαγαλλόμενος ‘exulting in’ takes the dative πολέμῳ καὶ δηϊοτῆτι ‘war and fighting’ (δηϊοτής is hostile fighting). ἐναιρόμενος is ‘slaying’. The object of ἡγεμονεύειν, the men he would lead, is not stated. μή τις … ἐμβήῃ is a fear clause with the aorist subjunctive of ἐμβαίνω ‘step in, set foot in’; the place stepped into is not said, and ‘step in’ is the sense of the context. Οὐλύμποιο is genitive of Olympus, ἀπ’ ‘from’. θεῶν αἰειγενετάων is ‘of the gods, the forever-born’, ‘of the everlasting gods’ in the English. The line breaks at the raised stop.

sentences.t: μάλα τούς γε φιλεῖ ἑκάεργος Ἀπόλλων·
sentences.l: very much them, at least, loves the far-working Apollo;
sentences.i: Apollo, who works from afar, loves them dearly;
sentences.n: τούς ‘them’ are the Trojans. μάλα … γε φιλεῖ is ‘loves greatly’, the particle γε stressing τούς. ἑκάεργος is a stock epithet of Apollo, translated every time; its meaning is disputed (‘far-working’ or ‘far-shooting’), and the English keeps the literal ‘far-working, who works from afar’. This is the reason for the warning of line 93.

sentences.t:
ἀλλὰ πάλιν τρωπᾶσθαι, ἐπὴν φάος ἐν νήεσσι
θήῃς, τοὺς δ’ ἔτ’ ἐᾶν πεδίον κάτα δηριάασθαι.
sentences.l:
but turn back, when light among the ships
you have set, and leave them still to fight over the plain.
sentences.i: but turn back once you have brought light to the ships, and leave the others to go on fighting over the plain.
sentences.n: ἀλλά after the prohibitions gives the instead: τρωπᾶσθαι, an infinitive as imperative, is ‘turn back’, with πάλιν ‘back’. ἐπήν is ‘when, once’, and θήῃς is the aorist subjunctive of τίθημι, ‘you have put’. φάος ‘light’ is relief and safety, as in 39. τοὺς δέ ‘but those’ are the others, who are to be left to the fighting; the Greek does not say which side. ἔτ’ ἐᾶν is ‘to let be still’, and δηριάασθαι is ‘to contend, fight’. πεδίον κάτα is κατὰ πεδίον ‘over the plain’, with the preposition set after its noun.

sentences.t:
αἲ γὰρ Ζεῦ τε πάτερ καὶ Ἀθηναίη καὶ Ἄπολλον
μήτέ τις οὖν Τρώων θάνατον φύγοι ὅσσοι ἔασι,
μήτέ τις Ἀργείων, νῶϊν δ’ ἐκδῦμεν ὄλεθρον,
ὄφρ’ οἶοι Τροίης ἱερὰ κρήδεμνα λύωμεν.
sentences.l:
Would that — Father Zeus, and Athena, and Apollo —
not any then of the Trojans might escape death, as many as there are,
and not any of the Argives, and for us two to slip out of destruction,
so that we alone might loosen the sacred head-veils of Troy.”
sentences.i: If only — Father Zeus, Athena, and Apollo — not one of the Trojans, however many there are, might escape death, and not one of the Argives, and the two of us might slip out of destruction, so that we alone might loosen the sacred head-veils of Troy.”
sentences.n: The first line stands word for word in Book 2 (iliad-011, where the next line differs). αἲ γάρ is the wish ‘if only’, and φύγοι (the aorist optative of φεύγω) ‘might escape’ has μήτε τις … μήτε τις ‘neither any … nor any’. ὅσσοι ἔασι is ‘as many as there are’ (ἔασι = εἰσί). νῶϊν δ’ ἐκδῦμεν is the dual dative ‘for us two’ with ἐκδῦμεν, an epic infinitive of ἐκδύω ‘slip out of’; it hangs on the same wish, and the English joins it to the wish as ‘might slip out’. The two are Achilles and Patroclus. οἶοι is ‘alone’, in the plural. λύωμεν is the subjunctive of λύω ‘loosen’ after ὄφρα ‘so that’. Τροίης ἱερὰ κρήδεμνα ‘the sacred head-veils of Troy’ is probably a figure for the city’s walls and towers (the sense is not certain), as in the Odyssey (13.388); ἱερά is ‘sacred’. The speech ends here, and the narrator takes it up.
